analysis.title: Weekly Mash - 30 Oct 2026 (Mark Wilson, FICC & Equities)
key_insights: Wilson had argued that hyperscaler results this week and the US midterms next week were peak event risk, with a year-end rally to follow. He says the last two weeks were bruising for that view, with two steps back for every step forward.

He calls the AI investment cycle the largest driver of macro markets. Other live items he lists are the Brazil election shock, Israeli election uncertainty, the UK budget, Middle East energy logistics, higher crude and European gas prices roughly doubling in three months.

Hyperscaler cloud growth is accelerating. Alphabet cloud revenue grew 103% y/y with backlog up 256% y/y ($120b ARR, $561b backlog). Azure grew 48%, held back by supply, with an acceleration expected next quarter. AWS grew 39% with backlog up 189% y/y to $578b, and management is confident in AWS growth above 40% in 2027 and 2028.
Wilson says the ROI question on hyperscaler capex is being answered. Management teams described a pull-forward of returns on growth capex, and Jassy noted 85% of global IT spend is still on premises.

Financing visibility improved. Meta completed the first two legs (common and convertible) of a three-part record equity raise. Oracle brought forward its cash flow breakeven forecast and said it needs only $20b of financing for its capex plans. 2026 capex plans stayed stable and 2027 expectations were little changed. US 10-year yields have fallen four weeks running.

Wilson sees a definitive bull market in cyber risk, driven by AI tooling and a larger attack surface. Binance suffered what he calls the largest heist in history late in the week. Jassy suggested security could be 20% or a significant share of token usage over the next year or two.

Nasdaq was down more than 3.5% on the day of writing, on bad news from Intel, concern about certain software names, and questions on Alphabet's search and Amazon's retail businesses. Wilson argues the market may judge the cloud, financing and cyber items differently in coming days and weeks.

The 'AI-winners vs AI-at-risk' basket pair traded a low-vol trend in the first half of the year and is now down on the year. Mag7 and hyperscaler outperformance versus the index, which began in late June, has been dented this week.
Stock correlations have broken down. Apple is now negatively correlated to the Nasdaq and S&P equal-weight has only a 60% correlation to the S&P 500.

The S&P ex-AI outperformed Nasdaq by more than 3% on the week and France's CAC beat US tech by 5%. The S&P 500 fell 30bps on a day when 80% of constituents rose, which Wilson describes as highly unusual.

No sign of AI demand slowing as of today. Token demand is accelerating and chip pricing, rental yields and useful-life duration are rising. Supply-side concerns center on capacity constraints rather than overbuild. Efficiency or power breakthroughs are possible in coming months.

Wilson says the neocloud credit story and 2007/2008 comparisons are misplaced, though the higher cost of capital did hamper equities. He frames the right question as whether this is 1997 or 1999. He cites Vickie Chang's work on macro assets in Fed hiking cycles, whose lesson is that three months of equity indigestion does not change the trend.

Quarter-on-quarter capex growth may have paused for now with a focus on efficiency gains. Wilson says this means more discretion is needed on 2027 winners, but reports of the AI capex demise and funding threat look greatly exaggerated.
He calls continued de-risking ahead of next week's midterms understandable, but says it magnifies the possible opportunity once known unknowns clear.

sector_views.rationale: Cloud growth and backlog are accelerating, financing gaps look smaller than feared, and capex payback is being cited by management. Wilson says more discretion is needed on 2027 winners.

earnings_insights: Alphabet Q3 2026 results reported this week: cloud revenue +103% y/y, revenue backlog +256% y/y ($120b ARR, $561b backlog). Reported figures as cited by GS, no consensus comparison given.

Microsoft reported this week: Azure growth of 48%, held back by supply constraints. Management expects an acceleration next quarter as supply improves. Copilot usage-based billing grew over 7% in the quarter and Copilot daily users rose nearly 50% q/q.

Amazon reported this week: AWS grew 39% in the quarter, backlog +189% y/y to $578b. Management expressed confidence in AWS growth above 40% in each of 2027 and 2028. Graviton and Trainium revenue commitments each rose more than 20x y/y.
Oracle financial update this week: forecast date for cash flow breakeven brought forward, and only $20b of financing needed to deliver intended capex plans.
Meta completed the first two legs (common and convertible) of a three-part record equity raise this week.
Wilson cites objectively bad news from Intel, concern about certain software names, and questions on Alphabet's search and Amazon's retail businesses as reasons for the Nasdaq drop on the day.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Wilson links lower yields to better news on the quantum and price of required AI financing.
Listed among the non-AI drivers of markets alongside higher crude and Middle East energy logistics complications.

crypto_views: Binance fell victim to what Wilson calls the largest heist in history late in the week, which he ties to the rising cyber risk from AI tooling and a larger attack surface.
risk_factors: A slowdown in AI demand or supply-side signs of excess capacity, which Wilson says are not visible today.
Power and compute efficiency breakthroughs could change the demand picture in coming months.
Higher cost of capital for AI financing, and neocloud credit concerns.
Core business questions for Alphabet's search and Amazon's retail, concern about certain software names, and bad news from Intel.
Rising cyber risk from AI tooling and a larger attack surface.
US midterms next week and broader event risk including elections abroad, the UK budget and Middle East energy logistics.
vol_and_positioning: The AI-winners vs AI-at-risk basket pair traded a remarkably low-vol trend through the first half of the year and is now down on the year, struggling for direction.
Mag7 and hyperscaler outperformance versus the index since late June has been dented this week.
Apple is now negatively correlated to the Nasdaq and S&P equal-weight has only a 60% correlation to the S&P 500.
The S&P 500 fell 30bps on a day when 80% of constituents were up, per GS US derivatives (Brian Garrett).
Investors have continued to de-risk ahead of the midterms, which Wilson says magnifies the possible opportunity as known unknowns clear.
geopolitical: Complications of Middle East energy logistics

tension_points.bull_case: Hyperscaler cloud growth and backlog are accelerating (Alphabet cloud +103%, AWS backlog +189%, Azure to re-accelerate), management cites capex payback and visibility into 2027 to 2029, financing gaps look smaller than feared, and 2026 capex plans were stable.
tension_points.bear_case: Higher cost of capital and neocloud credit concerns hampered equities in recent months. Core business questions remain for Alphabet search and Amazon retail, and software names and Intel were weak. The market sold off more than 3.5% on the Nasdaq despite the results.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A slowdown in AI demand or signs of supply-side excess capacity, which Wilson says is not detectable today.

theme_stances.key_argument: The return on hyperscaler spend is becoming clear, and reports of the AI capex demise and funding threat look greatly exaggerated.
theme_stances.evidence: the ROI on hyperscaler spend is revealing itself quite clearly

theme_stances.key_argument: The financing gap is significantly less than feared week on week, helped by Meta's raise, SpaceX's chip financing news and Oracle's guide.
theme_stances.evidence: the financing gap is significantly less than feared

theme_stances.key_argument: AI tooling and a larger attack surface have created rising cyber risk, shown by the Binance heist.
theme_stances.evidence: definitive bull market in cyber risk
